title: Picking up stitches along an edge
subtitle: Adding a border or band to a finished crochet piece by working into the side edge
excerpt: Picking up stitches along a row-end edge is the technique for adding a button band, a collar, or a decorative edging to a finished crochet piece without seaming on a separate strip. The stitches are worked directly into the side edge of the existing fabric.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776.

glossaryTerms.definition: The vertical edge of a flat crochet piece formed by the sides of each row, rather than the top or bottom. Button bands and side edgings are typically picked up from this edge.
The ratio of stitches picked up to rows (or stitches) along the edge. Different stitch heights require different rates to produce a flat band.

content.text: Picking up stitches along a
row-end edge

is how you add a button band, collar, or edging to a finished crochet piece without seaming on a separate strip. You work directly into the side edge of the existing fabric, catching one or two threads of each row end to anchor the new stitches.
The main challenge is the
rate of pickup
: how many stitches to pick up per row. Pick up too many and the band ruffles; too few and it pulls in. The correct rate depends on the height of the stitches in the original fabric.
What you need

items.name: Crochet hook
items.note: The same hook used for the main piece, or one size smaller if the band needs to be firmer

items.name: Stitch markers
items.note: Place at regular intervals along the edge to keep the pickup rate consistent

content.text: Rate of pickup by stitch type
These are approximate starting rates for flat fabric:
Double crochet (UK): 1 stitch per row end gives a flat band in most yarns.
Half treble (UK): 1 stitch per row end, occasionally 3 stitches per 2 row ends.
Treble (UK): 2 stitches per row end gives a flat band; 3 per 2 rows can also work.
Double treble (UK): 2 to 3 stitches per row end. The taller the stitch, the more pickup stitches it needs.
Step by step
Count the total number of rows along the edge. Divide by the pickup rate to calculate the expected number of stitches for the band.
Divide the edge into equal sections with stitch markers (every 10 rows, for example). This keeps the pickup rate consistent across the full length.
With the right side of the work facing you, insert the hook into the side of the first row end, under two threads. Yarn over and draw a loop through. This is one picked-up stitch.
Continue picking up stitches at the correct rate to the end of the edge.
Work the required number of rows for the band, then fasten off. Do not seam: the picked-up stitches are the join.
Common problems

items.symptom: The band is ruffling along the edge
items.cause: Too many stitches were picked up per row, causing the band to have more fabric than the edge can accommodate.
items.fix: Rip back the band and pick up fewer stitches. Start by reducing by 1 stitch every 5 rows and check the result on a swatch before re-working the full band.

items.symptom: The band is pulling in and making the edge curl
items.cause: Too few stitches were picked up, so the band is under tension.
items.fix: Rip back and pick up more stitches. Work a test swatch on a short section of edge before picking up along the full length.

items.symptom: The pickup row looks irregular with large gaps between stitches in some places
items.cause: The pickup was done without using section markers, so the rate drifted across the edge.
items.fix: On future pickups, divide the edge into equal sections with markers before starting. Work the same number of stitches in each section.

content.text: What to try next

A single row of double crochet (UK) picked up around the full perimeter of a simple square swatch is the standard test: it shows immediately whether the rate is right at the corners and the straight edges. Once the rate is reliable, a button band for a cardigan is the most common application.
